schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make the title govern the whole list of returnees under Zerubbabel and Joshua, the same register Nehemiah later incorporated; Ellicott traces 'children of the captivity' becoming 'children of the province,' every man to his city so far as it was known.

Clarke reads the province as Judea over against Babylon (behold the goodness and severity of God); Wesley hears the word 'province' spoken emphatically, to mark the sad fall from an independent kingdom to a servile dependency.

Henry makes the written account an honour and recompence to the faithful, sees how sin debases a nation righteousness would exalt, and reads the servitude as a reminder of the better country (Heb. 11:16).
Gill weighs Jarchi (province = Judea, a kingdom reduced) against Aben Ezra (province = Babylon where the exiles dwelt).

Gill identifies Jeshua as Joshua the high priest, reports Lightfoot's bold identifications of Nehemiah, Mordecai, and Seraiah (Ezra), but judges with others that they are different men of the same names.
Henry makes Zerubbabel and Jeshua the Moses and Aaron of the return, and thinks Nehemiah and Mordecai probably the same famous men, come now and afterward returned to court.
Keil sets the text beside its Nehemiah twin, noting the variance of names and numbers; Ellicott counts twelve leaders for the twelve tribes, one (Nahamani) wanting and three in altered forms.

Clarke marks three copies (Ezra, Nehemiah, Esdras) correcting one another, the total agreeing at 42,360 though the particulars fall short, with Alting's reconciliation; Wesley ascribes the divergence to multiple names and to changes over the years.

debates.question: Are the Nehemiah, Mordecai, and Seraiah named here the famous men of those names?

sides.position: probably the same famous men, who came now and returned to court afterward (Lightfoot identifying Seraiah with Ezra)
rather different men of the same names, since the famous Nehemiah and Mordecai belong to a later time

schools.summary: Clarke lays down the governing rule — 'children' before a man's name means his descendants, before a place its inhabitants; Wesley fixes 'children of Parosh' as his posterity, and so for the rest.
Gill describes the whole list as families set out by ancestor or town and by number, otherwise unknown.
Ellicott opens his family-by-family comparison of the three authorities; Parosh's 2,172 agrees in all, the divergences coming only further on.
Keil lists Shephatiah at 372, unchanged in Nehemiah 7:9; Ellicott reckons it among the numbers on which the three authorities do not part, an agreement that fixes the shape of the document.
Clarke holds the catalogue sure in its grand total, its three hands correcting one another, each family a real company though the particulars fall short.
Henry finds in the very keeping of such numbers a token of honour, written for the credit of the returning and the benefit of their posterity.

Wesley explains the gap between 775 and 652 as those who set out from Babylon against those who reached Jerusalem, some dying or hindered on the road; Clarke keeps the surplus-reconciliation of the three copies.
Keil records Arah at 775 against Nehemiah's 652, one of the larger differences, and takes such variations as the ordinary marks of hand-copied documents.

outliers.note: Explains the difference between Ezra's 775 and Nehemiah's 652 as the difference between those who marched out of Babylon and those who arrived at Jerusalem, some having died or been hindered on the way — a solution he offers once for all such cases.

themes: those who set out and those who arrived

schools.summary: Henry notes Adonikam ('a high lord') numbered 666, just the number of the beast (Rev. 13:18), and reports Hugh Broughton's thought that the Apocalypse's figure has reference to this man.
Keil sets 666 here against Nehemiah's 667; Ellicott finds both Nehemiah and Esdras correcting 666 into 667, so the famous number may be a copyist's slip.

debates.question: Is the 666 of Adonikam the firm reading, or a copyist's slip for 667?

sides.position: 666 stands, and strikingly matches the number of the beast (Broughton referring the Apocalypse's figure to this man)
667 is the true figure — two of the three witnesses correct 666, likely a scribal error

outliers.note: Passes on Hugh Broughton's conjecture that the number of the beast in Revelation 13:18 refers to this Adonikam whose house numbered 666 — offered as a curiosity, not doctrine.

schools.summary: Clarke reads the children of Bethlehem as the town's inhabitants; Wesley wonders that Bethlehem, so little among the thousands of Judah, should yet be the place whence the Messiah must arise, and extends the note to Netophah and Anathoth.
Henry marks the 123, small though it was David's city, as the setting of the wonder — there must the Messiah be born (Micah 5:2), God choosing the small and despised.

themes: little among the thousands of Judah

schools.summary: Clarke identifies Lod, Hadid, and Ono as cities of Benjamin (cf. 1 Chron. 8:12), their 'children' being inhabitants, not descendants of three men.
Ellicott marks the 725 here and in Esdras against Nehemiah's 721, the smaller figure the odd one out.
Gill keeps the character of the whole roll, families named by ancestor or town, of most of whom nothing more is known.

Henry finds the priests about a tenth of the whole — God's part, a blessed decimation — three of David's courses represented (1 Chron. 24:7), the fourth Pashur, strangely fruitful if of Jeremiah's persecutor.
Ellicott gives the priests by houses, three of the twenty-four courses represented, Pashur not among them, and reads 'of the house of Jeshua' of the serving high priest's race.
Gill counts four priestly families/courses totalling 4,289, all that returned from Babylon.
Clarke marks that the preceding census took Judah and Benjamin, and now the sacred tribe is told apart.

Keil records Immer at 1,052, firm across the witnesses (unlike the lay numbers), the four priestly houses agreeing at 4,289; Ellicott notes the priests' numbers large and steady, the sacred tribe least able to afford a slip.
Henry makes the priestly tenth a blessed decimation, yet mourns that only four of the twenty-four courses returned, the priesthood come home shrunken but sufficient.
Wesley names Harim head of one of David's twenty-four courses (1 Chron. 24:8), of which only four or five returned, and distinguishes this priestly Harim from the lay Harim named earlier.
Ellicott marks only three or four courses represented, their numbers (Harim's 1,017 among them) large beside the other classes.
Henry makes the whole priestly muster the tenth that is God's, a blessed decimation, mourning the courses that failed to come up.
Gill marks the Levites, singers, and porters together but 341, where in David's day they were 38,000.
Henry wonders at so few Levites (not 350 in all); once more forward than the priests, now they lagged — the wind blows where it lists.
Ellicott traces the Levites proper to two families under Hodaviah, only Asaph of the three choirs returning; Keil corrects the readings 'Kadmiel' and 'of Hodaviah' and attaches the clause to Kadmiel.

themes: so few of the ministering tribe

schools.summary: Keil notes only Asaph's choir returned, 128 here against Nehemiah's 148 (Bakbukiah elsewhere standing for Heman's order); Ellicott too finds only the sons of Asaph of the three great singing-houses.
Henry folds the singers into his wonder at the whole ministering remnant, singers and porters and Levites failing to make 350.

Keil names six porter families, three (Shallum, Talmon, Akkub) having kept Jerusalem's gates before the captivity (1 Chron. 9:17), the number 139 against Nehemiah's 138; Ellicott says the same of the six families, three in the old Jerusalem.
Henry counts the doorkeepers with the same reverence as the priests, the meanest office of the house being still an honour.
Gill takes the Nethinim ('the given ones') for the Gibeonites given by Joshua and by David to serve the Levites.
Wesley calls them persons devoted to the inferior services of the priests and Levites, commonly supposed the Gibeonites (Josh. 9:27).
Keil calls them temple-bondsmen, 35 families with 10 of Solomon's servants totalling 392, and lists the textual variants against Nehemiah.
Henry finds it an honour to belong to God's house though in the meanest office there.
Keil treats the long file together — 35 Nethinim families, 392 in all, only 8 or 9 to a household — and notes the parallel roll now diverging, the variations touching only the form of the words.
Gill keeps them the descendants of the Gibeonites devoted to the meaner services, of whom nothing survives but their names.
Wesley had fixed their office as the inferior services of priests and Levites, the light in which even this bare column is read.

themes: little families of the given ones

schools.summary: Keil counts these among the 35 Nethinim households (392 in all, 8 or 9 to a clan), the parallel roll now agreeing and now diverging, the differences the marks of a long-copied text.
Gill keeps them the descendants of the Gibeonites given to the sanctuary, only bare names now surviving.
Henry's word — an honour to belong to God's house though in the meanest office — redeems the dryness of the roll.

themes: God forgets none of his servants

schools.summary: Clarke takes Solomon's servants for those appointed to the meaner services; Wesley says they lived in Solomon's household and gloried afterward in the name of servants to so great a prince.

Ellicott makes them the remnant of the Canaanites (1 Kings 9:21), inferior to the Nethinim yet faithful to their inherited service and valued when the Levites were few; Keil counts ten such houses among the 392.

themes: the servants of the servants remembered

schools.summary: Henry makes the company that could not prove itself Israelite yet went up out of affection a rebuke to the true-born who had lost their relish for the waters of Judah (Isa. 48:1).
Gill fixes Tel-melah and Tel-harsa as towns in the land of Babylon whence the doubtful company came.
Keil sets the families who could not show their Israelite descent before the priests whose genealogy likewise could not be found.

themes: a rebuke to the Israelite in name only

schools.summary: Gill marks that though their nearer parents were known, these houses could carry the genealogy no further, nor show the father's house or tribe.
Keil records the 652 and ranks the three houses with those who could not prove their membership of Israel, the parallel differing a little.
Henry keeps up the reflection — presuming themselves of Jacob's seed, unable to produce pedigrees, yet going up out of affection to the house and people of God.

Keil names Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai, unable to find their registers (Hakkoz a course-name but insufficient alone), and tells how a priest took the name of Barzillai the Gileadite for the inheritance; Ellicott corrects 'after her name,' she being probably an heiress (2 Sam. 17:27).
Gill notes simply that these priests could not make out their pedigree, unlike those named before.
Henry makes them a warning — preferring an honourable alliance to the priesthood, they sold their birthright for gentility and were justly degraded; Christ is ashamed of those ashamed of him.

themes: priests who could not prove their line
a name and inheritance preferred to the priesthood

schools.summary: Ellicott renders it the record of the enregistered, 'polluted' meaning Levitically disqualified; Keil carries it to the governor's ban from the most holy things until the matter be resolved.
Gill explains the public registers of the priests, their descent and marriages kept that the fit might be known from the unfit.
Wesley enlarges on the exactness of the Jewish genealogies — for offices, inheritances, and marriages, and by God's providence that the Messiah's tribe and family might be certainly known.

themes: put from the priesthood as polluted
the record that would vindicate Christ

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the Tirshatha (Pechah, 'the feared') Zerubbabel, and notes the Urim and Thummim never again inquired of; Keil too names Zerubbabel the secular governor deferring the matter.

Clarke supposes the Tirshatha Nehemiah or the commandant, the Urim lost in the captivity; Wesley makes him Zerubbabel and reads the want of the oracle as teaching the people to expect the Messiah, the great Oracle.
Gill weighs Jarchi (Tirshatha = Nehemiah) against Aben Ezra (a title of honour = Zerubbabel the prince), preferring the latter.

debates.question: Who is the Tirshatha of this verse — Nehemiah or Zerubbabel?

sides.position: Nehemiah, or the commandant of the day, the word being an official title
Zerubbabel, the prince and governor of the return

schools.summary: Keil sets the three totals side by side — the grand total 42,360 in all, but the particulars 29,818 (Ezra), 31,089 (Nehemiah), and another in Esdras — owing the differences to clerical errors; Ellicott too thinks errors crept into the documents, noting Esdras's remark that children under twelve were not reckoned.
Henry supposes the twelve thousand unaccounted of the other tribes, and marvels that the returning host was more than double those carried captive, a little one become a thousand.
Gill reckons the particulars at 29,829, the missing twelve thousand being of the other tribes.
Wesley allows the 12,542 added into the total were either of the other tribes or of unprovable pedigree.

debates.question: Why do the itemised sums fall short of the grand total of 42,360 (and differ between Ezra and Nehemiah)?

sides.position: the total is right and includes the unnamed thousands of the other ten tribes, whom the lists (confined to Judah and Benjamin) left out
the total is fixed and true, but the itemised sums have suffered clerical and transcription errors in copying

themes: the other ten tribes or copyists' errors
a little one become a thousand

schools.summary: Keil records the 7,337 servants and the 200 singers, rejecting Michaelis's 'oxen and cows' emendation; Ellicott reports the Rabbis' explanation, notes singers were hired for lamentation too and may have supplied the lack of Levites (Nehemiah's 245).
Gill reads the few servants as a mark of the returning people's poverty.
Henry takes the 200 as meant to excite the people's grief, for they should come home weeping (Jer. 50:4).

outliers.note: Report, only to reject, Michaelis's conjecture that '200 singing men and women' was originally 'oxen and cows,' the objection being that the word for cows is nothing like that for singing-women.

themes: two hundred singing men and women

schools.summary: Gill reads the few horses and mules as a mark of poverty, most walking home on foot, and notes the Latin variant of 636 horses.
Keil notes the beasts stand at identical figures in Nehemiah, though Esdras differs, naming the camels first.
Clarke turns the tally to praise — a people once stripped in captivity now returning abounding in substantial riches.
Keil notes the camels and asses at the same figures as in Nehemiah; Ellicott observes the ass throughout Hebrew history the chief and most numerous beast of burden.
Clarke keeps the note that a people once stripped now returned abounding in substantial riches, their camels and asses in hundreds and thousands.

themes: the ass the beast of burden

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil agree the chief fathers came to the bare site of the house not yet built and brought free-will offerings to set it up in its place, after their ability.
Gill notes they came to the place where the temple had stood, amid its ruins.
Henry likens them to Abraham coming to the place of the altar when the altar was gone (Gen. 13:4), offering freely though newly come off the march and beginning the world anew.

themes: the site of the ruined house
first love of the returning people

schools.summary: Clarke reckons the darics and manehs near £120,000 and sees God's mercy in the captivity; Wesley cites Cumberland, the silver about £37,000.

Keil gives the darics above £68,000 and the silver above £30,000 but calls Nehemiah's account more exact; Ellicott judges Nehemiah more correct and this text's 61,000 a corruption of 41,000, the rest round numbers.
Gill explains the drams as Persian gold darics, the whole 45,000 to 61,000 pounds.
Henry sets the gift, given by drams not by talents as in David's day (1 Chron. 29:7), as acceptable to God as those talents, like the widow's two mites.
Clarke has each house return to the city of its family; Wesley marks that they dwelt in peace and perfect unity, a blessed presage of their settlement.
Ellicott hears in 'all Israel in their cities' a note of triumph — no partial affair but a national revival, though Judah and Benjamin furnished the most.
Henry finds them content in their ruined cities, room enough and no strife, and reads the homecoming as a shadow of the gospel return to the holy city of God.
Gill notes the cities were those assigned them, where they or their forefathers had dwelt before the captivity.

themes: the homecoming a shadow of the gospel
